units.translation: having cast upon the city an unbearable pollution.
the unbearable child of forethought, Ruin.
a storm — such as the unbearable snow of Ida produced.
an unbearable evil to his friends.
and he prays for an unbearable doom upon the Pelopids.
seeking to establish an unbearable doom for your life.
let loose to wander at the farthest boundaries of the earth.
and you will bear a dark Epaphus, named after the touches of Zeus (thus Wieseler for 'of the offspring').

I have restored ἀφημένων [those sitting apart] for αφεμένων [those having been sent away], on which see the Preface to the fifth Leipzig edition p. XCI. The verb ἀφίεσθαι [to be sent away] is not suitable to this passage. For Menelaus was not dismissed by Helen, but deserted by her sits at home without glory, which is signified by the verb ἀφῆσθαι [to sit apart].
somewhere by the guidance of a voiceless informer.
and the light of fire called imperishable.
you persuaded the immortal Fates to make mortals deathless.
he who ate the ever-living, imperishable grass.
and I stood speechless with fear.
it is the law that the murderer be voiceless.
but the unenvied man is not enviable.
not exposed to envy; abundant, plentiful

ριο ἀφθονωτέραν [more abundant], in Athenaeus 10 p. 424d, where examples of similar comparatives are adduced. In the Venetian codex is ἀφθονέστερα [more abundant things], which Casaubon corrected. The Epitomator wrote ἀφθονέστερον [more abundantly].
and they send, kindling with abundant force of flame, a great beard of fire.
and reveal this name with ungrudging speech.
self-sown fields bring abundant livelihood to mortals.
In which sense ἀφοσιοῦσθαι [to purify oneself] is used.
long ago we were purified of these things in other houses.
to send, let go; to leave
[ἀφεμένων [those having been sent away] erroneously for ἀφημένων [those sitting apart]. See ἄφημαι.]
let go of the anger you have.
and the soft-robed beds, the delight of luxurious youth, having abandoned them.
having shed the drops of the gods.
O foot, I will let you go.
having left the deep-soiled land to their enemies.
or have you come to view my fortunes?
and you will come to the nomadic Scythians,
nor does any horseman arrive at the city of the Persians.
arms and ashes arrive at each man's house.
in the tenth year I have come to this light.
to what kinder land than this could we come?
I have come to a day of lofty cliffs.
we have come to the land of the Macedonians.
according to the laws of suppliants.
may Zeus, protector of suppliants, look kindly upon our expedition.
